subject: biology

items.q: A cut in the skin heals as new skin cells are produced by cell division. Why must DNA replication take place before each of these divisions?
items.correct: So that each new cell receives a complete copy of the DNA with an identical base sequence.
items.misconception: So that the existing DNA can be divided equally, half going to each of the new cells.
items.why: Cell division is described as a cell 'splitting in two', and the cytoplasm really is divided between the daughter cells. Students extend this halving to the DNA, especially having met the halving of chromosome number in meiosis. DNA replication produces exact copies of the DNA before division, so each daughter cell receives a complete set of DNA with the same base sequence as the parent cell, not half of it.
items.specStatementText: Replication makes exact copies, and every dividing cell needs it
items.random_wrong: It does not need to take place, because replication is only required for reproduction.

items.q: During replication, a section of a template strand with the base sequence TACGGA is copied. Which statement describes the new strand built on this section?
items.correct: Its sequence is ATGCCT, the complement of the template, held to it by hydrogen bonds.
items.misconception: Its sequence is TACGGA, an exact copy of the template strand it was assembled on.
items.why: Replication is described as 'copying' the DNA, so students expect the new strand to copy the template directly. The fact that the identical copy is of the template's original partner, not of the template itself, is a step further than the word 'copy' suggests. Complementary base pairing means each new strand has the sequence complementary to its template. Because the two original strands were themselves complementary, each daughter molecule ends up with exactly the same pair of sequences as the parent molecule.
items.specStatementText: Each copy keeps one old strand; base pairing keeps the copy accurate
items.random_wrong: Its sequence is AUGCCU, because uracil replaces thymine in each newly made strand.

items.q: Bacteria were grown for many generations with only heavy nitrogen (¹⁵N), so all their DNA was heavy. They were then moved to a medium with only light nitrogen (¹⁴N). After one round of replication, all the DNA had a density midway between heavy and light. After a second round, half the DNA was of this intermediate density and half was light. What do these results show about replication?
items.correct: Each daughter molecule keeps one original strand and gains one strand that is newly made.
items.misconception: The original double-stranded molecule stays intact and a completely new molecule is made beside it.
items.why: In everyday life a copy leaves the original untouched, as with a photocopy. Diagrams that show 'the parent DNA' and 'the copy' as two separate molecules reinforce the idea that one of the products is the intact original. The two strands of the original molecule separate and each acts as a template for a new strand. Each daughter molecule therefore keeps one original strand and gains one new strand, which is why replication is called semi-conservative.
items.specStatementText: Each copy keeps one old strand; base pairing keeps the copy accurate
items.random_wrong: Old and new nucleotides become mixed along both strands of every daughter molecule.

items.q: What is the role of helicase in DNA replication?
items.correct: It unwinds the double helix and breaks the hydrogen bonds between the two strands.
items.misconception: It cuts through the sugar–phosphate backbone so that the two strands can come apart.
items.why: Enzymes met earlier, such as digestive enzymes and restriction enzymes, break covalent bonds and 'cut' molecules, and the language of 'unzipping' and 'breaking bonds' does not say which bonds. Students do not picture the two strands as being held together only by hydrogen bonds. Helicase unwinds the helix and breaks only the hydrogen bonds between the paired bases. Each strand keeps its sugar–phosphate backbone intact, which is essential because the intact strands are the templates for replication.
items.specStatementText: Helicase opens the helix; DNA polymerase builds the new strands
items.random_wrong: It adds free nucleotides to each exposed template strand to assemble the two new strands.

items.q: A drug inhibits helicase but has no effect on DNA polymerase. What will happen to DNA replication in a cell treated with the drug?
items.correct: Replication cannot begin, because the hydrogen bonds between the strands are not broken, so no template strand is exposed.
items.misconception: Replication continues normally, because DNA polymerase unwinds the double helix itself as it copies each strand.
items.why: Both enzymes are learned as a pair with unfamiliar names, and 'polymerase' is not obviously linked to building a polymer. Some students reason that the enzyme named after DNA must be the one that handles the double helix. Helicase unwinds the double helix and breaks the hydrogen bonds between the strands. DNA polymerase then links free nucleotides into a new strand on each exposed template, following the rules of complementary base pairing.
items.specStatementText: Helicase opens the helix; DNA polymerase builds the new strands
items.random_wrong: New strands are made but fall off the template, because helicase forms the hydrogen bonds that hold new bases in place.

items.q: Why is Taq polymerase, rather than a DNA polymerase from human cells, used in the polymerase chain reaction?
items.correct: It is not denatured at the high temperature used to separate the strands, so it lasts through every cycle.
items.misconception: It is a bacterial enzyme that copies DNA much faster than a human polymerase, so fewer cycles are needed.
items.why: Students learn 'Taq polymerase' as a name to remember without linking it to its source, the hot-spring bacterium Thermus aquaticus. Speed seems the obvious reason to use a special enzyme in a technique whose purpose is to make many copies quickly. Every PCR cycle heats the mixture to about 95°C, which would denature a normal DNA polymerase. Taq polymerase, from a bacterium that lives in hot springs, keeps its shape at this temperature, so one addition of enzyme lasts for all the cycles.
items.specStatementText: PCR copies a chosen DNA section; electrophoresis sorts fragments by length
items.random_wrong: It separates the two strands of the template by itself, so no helicase has to be added to the reaction mixture.

items.q: What is the role of the primers in the polymerase chain reaction?
items.correct: They bind to sequences either side of the target, giving the polymerase a start point and defining the region copied.
items.misconception: They break the hydrogen bonds between the two strands so that the polymerase can reach the template.
items.why: PCR is taught as replication in a test tube, so students transfer every component of cellular replication into the reaction, including helicase. Heat as a way of breaking hydrogen bonds is less familiar than an enzyme doing the job. PCR uses temperature changes instead of helicase: heating to about 95°C breaks the hydrogen bonds and separates the strands. This is why a heat-stable DNA polymerase is needed.
items.specStatementText: PCR copies a chosen DNA section; electrophoresis sorts fragments by length
items.random_wrong: They only speed the reaction up, because Taq polymerase could begin a new strand at any point along the bare template.

items.q: A PCR reaction starts with 10 double-stranded DNA molecules of the target section. How many double-stranded molecules of the target are present after 3 complete cycles?
items.why: Students treat 'a copy per cycle' as an additive rate, as they would for most repeated processes, and reach for multiplication by the number of cycles rather than repeated doubling of the whole population. Every molecule present is copied in every cycle, so the total doubles each time. Starting from one molecule, 3 cycles give 8, 10 cycles give 1024 and 30 cycles give over a billion copies.
items.specStatementText: PCR copies a chosen DNA section; electrophoresis sorts fragments by length

items.q: Three DNA fragments of 200, 500 and 1200 base pairs are loaded into the same well of a gel and a voltage is applied. Which statement describes the result?
items.correct: The 200 base pair fragment moves furthest through the gel, towards the positive electrode.
items.misconception: The 1200 base pair fragment moves furthest, because it carries the most negative charge and is pulled harder.
items.why: Students reason from the electrical force alone: a longer fragment has more phosphate groups and more charge. They do not consider that charge per unit length is the same for every fragment and that the gel resists longer molecules more. All DNA fragments have the same charge per nucleotide, so the force per unit length is the same. Separation happens because the gel acts as a sieve: small fragments move through its pores faster and further, large fragments are held back.
items.specStatementText: PCR copies a chosen DNA section; electrophoresis sorts fragments by length
items.random_wrong: The 200 base pair fragment moves furthest, towards the negative electrode at the far end of the gel.

items.q: A DNA profile was prepared for a mother, her child and a man who may be the father. The fragment lengths (in base pairs) in each profile were: mother 100, 220, 260, 340; child 100, 150, 220, 300; man 150, 180, 300, 330. What can be concluded?
items.correct: The man cannot be excluded as the father: the child's two bands not from the mother (150 and 300) are both in his profile.
items.misconception: The man is excluded as the father, because two of his bands (180 and 330) do not appear in the child's profile.
items.why: Forensic matching, where a crime-scene sample should match a suspect's profile completely, is met first and applied to paternity. Students forget that a child inherits only half its DNA from each parent, so shares only half its bands with each. A child inherits one allele at each marker from each parent. The child's bands that are not explained by the mother must all appear in the father's profile; bands in the father that the child did not inherit are expected.
items.specStatementText: Using PCR and electrophoresis: DNA profiling in forensics and paternity
items.random_wrong: The man is excluded as the father, because the child's profile does not match his profile completely.

items.q: A forensic laboratory compares a sample from a crime scene with a suspect's DNA using 20 different markers rather than one. Why does this make the result more reliable?
items.correct: Each extra independent marker multiplies down the chance that an unrelated person matches by coincidence.
items.misconception: One marker is already conclusive, because everyone's DNA is unique; extra markers only make the bands easier to read.
items.why: Television and news coverage present DNA evidence as absolute proof, and 'everyone's DNA is unique' is taught as a fact. Students transfer the uniqueness of a whole genome to the few markers actually examined in a profile. Each marker is shared by a proportion of the population, so a single marker match is common. Using many independent markers multiplies the chances of coincidence together, making a false match extremely unlikely, but the result is a probability, not proof.
items.specStatementText: Using PCR and electrophoresis: DNA profiling in forensics and paternity
items.random_wrong: Testing 20 markers is equivalent to repeating a single marker 20 times, and repeating a measurement makes it more accurate.

items.q: During replication, how does DNA polymerase add each new nucleotide to the strand it is building?
items.correct: It joins the 5' phosphate of the incoming nucleotide to the 3' terminal of the growing strand, so the strand grows in the 5' to 3' direction.
items.misconception: It joins the 3' hydroxyl of the incoming nucleotide to the 5' terminal of the growing strand, so that the strand grows in the 3' to 5' direction.
items.why: The template is read in the 3' to 5' direction, and diagrams label the template more prominently than the new strand, so the direction of reading is taken as the direction of synthesis. Students also muddle which terminal carries the phosphate and which the hydroxyl. The template is read 3' to 5', but the new strand grows 5' to 3'. The 5' phosphate of the incoming nucleotide bonds to the 3' hydroxyl of the last nucleotide in the strand, so the growing end is the 3' terminal.
items.specStatementText: Strands have 5' and 3' ends, and polymerase builds one way only
items.random_wrong: It adds to whichever terminal faces the fork, so both new strands grow in the same direction as the replication fork moves.

items.q: Which statement correctly compares replication on the leading strand with replication on the lagging strand?
items.correct: The leading strand is made continuously towards the fork; the lagging strand discontinuously, as Okazaki fragments.
items.misconception: The leading strand is made in the 5' to 3' direction, while the lagging strand is made in the opposite, 3' to 5', direction.
items.why: Students know one strand is 'different' and that the polymerase works in one direction, so they conclude the difference must be the direction of synthesis. Diagrams showing the lagging strand fragments pointing 'backwards' reinforce this. DNA polymerase only ever adds nucleotides to a 3' terminal, so both strands are built 5' to 3'. On the lagging strand this direction points away from the fork, which is why the strand can only be built in short fragments as more template is exposed.
items.specStatementText: Leading strand is built continuously, lagging strand in fragments
items.random_wrong: Both new strands are made continuously towards the fork, because the two template strands run in the same direction.

items.q: Starting from the origin, one replication fork in a bacterium copies a 6000 base pair section of the chromosome. Okazaki fragments in this bacterium are about 1000 nucleotides long. Approximately how many RNA primers are needed at this fork?
items.correct: About seven: one on the leading strand plus one for each of the six or so Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand.
items.misconception: One: replication has to be initiated with an RNA primer only once, at the origin, for the whole fork.
items.why: The primer is introduced as the thing that 'starts' replication, and replication starts once. Students do not connect the need for a primer to each new fragment on the lagging strand, each of which is a fresh start for DNA polymerase. DNA polymerase cannot begin a strand, so every fragment needs its own primer. The leading strand is one continuous strand and needs one primer; the lagging strand is made of many Okazaki fragments and needs a primer for each.
items.specStatementText: Leading strand is built continuously, lagging strand in fragments
items.random_wrong: Two: one to start each of the two new strands, which are both built continuously to the end of the section.

items.q: What is the function of DNA polymerase I in prokaryotic DNA replication?
items.correct: It removes the RNA nucleotides of each primer and replaces them with DNA nucleotides, filling the gap.
items.misconception: It synthesizes most of the new DNA on both strands, being the first polymerase to act at the fork.
items.why: The Roman numerals record the order of discovery, not importance or sequence of action, but students naturally read 'I' as the primary enzyme. Having then learned that polymerase III is the main one, some swing to crediting it with everything. DNA polymerase III extends primers to build the leading strand and every Okazaki fragment, and proofreads its own additions. DNA polymerase I removes the RNA primers and replaces them with DNA. Neither does the other's job.
items.specStatementText: Four prokaryotic enzymes: primase, polymerase III, polymerase I, ligase
items.random_wrong: It joins the sugar–phosphate backbones of adjacent Okazaki fragments to make one continuous lagging strand.

items.q: On the lagging strand, DNA polymerase III has extended an Okazaki fragment until it reaches the RNA primer of the previous fragment. Which sequence of events completes this section of the strand?
items.correct: DNA polymerase I replaces the RNA primer with DNA nucleotides, and then DNA ligase joins the two fragments together.
items.misconception: DNA ligase joins the new fragment to the RNA primer, and then DNA polymerase I replaces the primer with DNA nucleotides.
items.why: 'Ligase' means 'joining enzyme', and joining nucleotides is what building a strand involves, so its job is blurred with that of DNA polymerase. Students also picture the fragments as needing to be joined as soon as they meet. DNA polymerase III joins nucleotides into a strand. DNA ligase acts only after DNA polymerase I has replaced the RNA primer with DNA, forming the single covalent bond that links the last nucleotide of one fragment to the first of the next.
items.specStatementText: Four prokaryotic enzymes: primase, polymerase III, polymerase I, ligase
items.random_wrong: DNA polymerase III removes the RNA primer and replaces it with DNA nucleotides, and then DNA ligase joins the two fragments.

items.q: As DNA polymerase III builds a new strand it adds a nucleotide carrying G opposite a T on the template. What happens next?
items.correct: DNA polymerase III removes the G nucleotide from the 3' terminal and adds an A in its place.
items.misconception: Synthesis continues, and the mismatch is found and corrected once the whole molecule has been copied.
items.why: 'Proofreading' in everyday use means reading through a finished piece of writing to find mistakes, so students imagine a scan of the completed DNA. This is also how repair processes met later are described. Proofreading happens nucleotide by nucleotide during synthesis. DNA polymerase III can only remove the nucleotide at the 3' terminal of the growing strand, so a mismatch must be caught immediately, before the next nucleotide is added.
items.specStatementText: Polymerase III checks each nucleotide as it adds it
items.random_wrong: DNA polymerase III removes the mismatched nucleotide from the 5' terminal of the new strand and replaces it.

items.q: A mutant strain of Escherichia coli has a DNA polymerase III that can add nucleotides normally but cannot remove them. Which prediction about this strain is correct?
items.correct: Its mutation rate rises, because mismatched nucleotides at the 3' terminal are left in place and copied in later replications.
items.misconception: Nothing changes, because complementary base pairing on its own ensures that every nucleotide added is correct.
items.why: Base pairing is taught as a strict rule (A always with T, G always with C), so students assume the rule cannot be broken. They have not met the idea that a wrong nucleotide can occasionally be held in position for long enough to be added. Base pairing greatly reduces errors but does not eliminate them. Proofreading by DNA polymerase III removes most of the mismatches that do occur; the few that remain are a source of mutation.
items.specStatementText: Polymerase III checks each nucleotide as it adds it
items.random_wrong: Nothing changes, because DNA polymerase I proofreads the new strand once DNA polymerase III has finished with it.

items.q: When does DNA replication take place in a multicellular organism?
items.correct: Before every cell division, so it is needed for growth and for the replacement of worn or damaged tissue, as well as for reproduction.
items.misconception: DNA replication only happens when an organism reproduces, because replication is about passing DNA on to offspring.
items.why: The words 'replicate' and 'reproduce' sound alike, and replication is first met alongside inheritance. Growth is pictured as cells getting bigger rather than as cells dividing, so the need to copy DNA for every new body cell is not seen. Every cell produced by cell division needs a complete copy of the DNA, so DNA replication is required for growth and tissue replacement in multicellular organisms, not only for reproduction.
items.specStatementText: Replication makes exact copies, and every dividing cell needs it
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is the product of DNA replication?
items.correct: DNA: two double-stranded DNA molecules with base sequences identical to the original.
items.misconception: DNA replication makes a copy of the DNA in the form of RNA, with uracil in place of thymine, so replication and transcription are the same process.
items.why: Both replication and transcription are introduced as 'copying' DNA using complementary base pairing, and both are taught in the same unit. The student attaches the one difference they remember, U for T, to every copying process. Replication produces DNA with the identical base sequence (A, T, C, G) to the original, using DNA nucleotides. Transcription is a different process that produces RNA from one gene. Only DNA is passed to daughter cells.
items.specStatementText: Replication makes exact copies, and every dividing cell needs it
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In a daughter DNA molecule, where are the original nucleotides found?
items.correct: All in one strand: one whole strand is original and the other whole strand is new.
items.misconception: Original and new nucleotides are mixed along both strands of each daughter molecule (dispersive replication).
items.why: Diagrams of replication show the new strand being built in pieces, and HL students meet Okazaki fragments, so the products are imagined as patchworks of old and new material rather than as whole conserved strands. Each original strand stays intact as a template. The new strand built on it is made entirely of new nucleotides, so a daughter molecule is one complete original strand paired with one complete new strand.
items.specStatementText: Each copy keeps one old strand; base pairing keeps the copy accurate
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which bonds does DNA polymerase form as it builds a new strand?
items.correct: Covalent bonds between the sugar of one nucleotide and the phosphate of the next, linking nucleotides into the growing strand; the hydrogen bonds to the template form spontaneously between complementary bases.
items.misconception: The enzymes of replication form the hydrogen bonds that hold each new nucleotide to its complementary base on the template.
items.why: Students learn that enzymes 'join' molecules and that base pairing is the central event of replication, so they assign the base pairing to the enzyme. Hydrogen bonds are rarely described as forming on their own. Complementary bases pair and form hydrogen bonds spontaneously when a free nucleotide is in position on the template. DNA polymerase catalyses the covalent bond that adds the nucleotide to the growing strand.
items.specStatementText: Helicase opens the helix; DNA polymerase builds the new strands
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why are primers needed in PCR?
items.correct: DNA polymerase can only extend an existing strand, not start one, so primers give it a starting point; because they bind to sequences either side of the target, they also define which section is amplified.
items.misconception: Primers are an optional extra that speed up PCR; the polymerase could start copying at any point on a bare single-stranded template without them.
items.why: The general role of DNA polymerase is described as 'building a new strand on a template', which gives no hint that the enzyme needs a starting strand. 'Primer' in everyday use means a preparatory coat, so it sounds inessential. A DNA polymerase cannot begin a strand on its own. In PCR, two short DNA primers anneal to complementary sequences flanking the target region; Taq polymerase extends each primer, and only the region between the primers is amplified.
items.specStatementText: PCR copies a chosen DNA section; electrophoresis sorts fragments by length
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Towards which electrode do DNA fragments move in gel electrophoresis?
items.correct: Towards the positive electrode, because DNA is negatively charged owing to its phosphate groups.
items.misconception: DNA fragments move towards the negative electrode.
items.why: Students either assume DNA is positively charged, or confuse which electrode is which, or remember that the samples are loaded at the negative end and assume the DNA belongs there. The phosphate groups of the backbone are not connected with charge. Each phosphate group in the sugar–phosphate backbone carries a negative charge, so DNA is negatively charged and moves away from the negative electrode, towards the positive electrode.
items.specStatementText: PCR copies a chosen DNA section; electrophoresis sorts fragments by length
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What property of DNA fragments does gel electrophoresis separate them by?
items.correct: Their length (number of base pairs).
items.misconception: Gel electrophoresis separates fragments by their base sequence, or reveals the base sequence of the DNA.
items.why: Electrophoresis is met alongside DNA profiling and 'reading' DNA, so the banding pattern is taken to be a readout of the sequence. Students also assume any technique that analyses DNA must be looking at bases. Fragments of the same length travel the same distance whatever their sequence. The gel separates by size only; the positions of the bands tell you fragment lengths, not the order of bases.
items.specStatementText: PCR copies a chosen DNA section; electrophoresis sorts fragments by length

items.q: Why does using more markers make a DNA profile more reliable?
items.correct: Each additional independent marker multiplies the probability of a chance match by a further small fraction, so the probability of a false match falls with every marker added.
items.misconception: Re-running the same marker several times improves reliability in the same way as testing several different markers.
items.why: The NOS statement that reliability improves with more measurements is applied literally as 'repeat the measurement'. Students do not distinguish repeating one test, which only checks for procedural error, from adding independent tests, which reduces the chance of coincidental agreement. Repeating one marker gives the same fragment lengths each time and does not change the chance that an unrelated person shares them. Testing additional independent markers is what reduces the probability of a false match.
items.specStatementText: Using PCR and electrophoresis: DNA profiling in forensics and paternity
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are the two new strands at a replication fork built in the same way?
items.correct: No. The two template strands are antiparallel and DNA polymerase works only 5' to 3', so one new strand is built continuously towards the fork and the other discontinuously, away from it.
items.misconception: The two strands of DNA run in the same direction, so both new strands are built in the same way, continuously towards the fork.
items.why: Simplified diagrams draw the two strands as parallel straight lines and show both new strands growing behind the fork like a zip closing. The antiparallel arrangement is a detail that has no consequence until directionality of polymerase is introduced. The strands are antiparallel. Because DNA polymerase can only add to a 3' terminal, only one template can be copied continuously towards the fork; the other is copied in short Okazaki fragments away from the fork.
items.specStatementText: Strands have 5' and 3' ends, and polymerase builds one way only
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is the primer made of, and which enzyme makes it?
items.correct: The primer is a short strand of RNA, made by DNA primase.
items.misconception: The primer is made of DNA, synthesized by a DNA polymerase, because the enzyme is called DNA primase.
items.why: The name 'DNA primase' suggests an enzyme that makes DNA, and in PCR the primers really are DNA. Students do not see why a cell would insert RNA into a DNA molecule. In cells the primer is RNA. DNA primase makes it because no DNA polymerase can start a strand; the RNA is later removed by DNA polymerase I and replaced with DNA.
items.specStatementText: Four prokaryotic enzymes: primase, polymerase III, polymerase I, ligase
